To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) harvesting to extinction can occur when a species’ range shrinks as its abundance declines and this is especially likely for species that school, herd, or flock; and (ii) this threat may be widespread, especially among terrestrial mammals and birds.

(1) harvesting to extinction is a threat to many species that are harvested for high value products, (2) harvesting to extinction occurs when harvesting costs do not increase as populations decline, (3) harvesting to extinction can be prevented if harvesting incentives diminish as populations decline, and (4) harvesting to extinction may be more likely to occur among species that have a limited range that contracts as populations decline, such as those that are schooling or patchily distributed.

(i) species can be driven to extinction by profitable harvesting if the range in which they live contracts as their populations decline; (ii) this threat is likely to be especially severe for terrestrial species, because range contractions may often occur in terrestrial populations; and (iii) the range contractions may occur because of patchy environments, schooling or flocking behavior, and climate-change impacts.

the economic theory of extinction, and it shows how a simple economic model can be used to identify and evaluate extinction risks.

the range contractions of some declining species can enable overharvesting to extinction, even if the price of the species does not rise, whereas the price increases of other declining species can enable extinction even if their range does not contract.
range contraction is an underappreciated extinction risk for harvested species.
the threat of overharvesting to extinction is greater for species that experience range contractions as abundance declines than for species that do not.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
harvesting to extinction can occur even if harvesters are rational, if harvest costs do not increase as populations decline.

the risk of overharvesting to extinction is not only driven by the market demand for a product (which is often the focus of conservation efforts), but also driven by the range contractions that may occur in declining populations.
range contractions, which are often overlooked as a cause of overharvesting extinction threats, are common enough to be a significant threat for some declining species.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the geographic area occupied by a declining species can play a larger role than the price of the harvested product in maintaining incentives to harvest to extinction, and this role may be especially large for terrestrial species.
range contractions can cause extinction-enabling declines in harvest costs.
factors causing range contraction, including schooling and patchy environments, may pose unexpectedly large threats to harvested species, and therefore merit greater attention.
